title: Characterizing Precision Nutrition Discourse on Twitter: Quantitative Content Analysis
screen_reason: Quantitative content analysis of 504 coded tweets about nutrigenetics/nutrigenomics captured 1 Sep - 1 Dec 2020. Two subject-matter experts double-coded every tweet for 'potentially misleading' vs 'incorrect (untrue)' information, fact-checking where needed. The paper reports 14.9% (75/504) untrue and 29% (146/504) potentially misleading - shares of items in a sample explicitly coded false/misleading against expert fact-checking, with a stated denominator, i.e. CONTENT prevalence.

estimates.country: Not stated (English-language tweets, no country restriction; authors are US-based)
estimates.measure_type: % of coded precision-nutrition tweets containing untrue (false) information
estimates.denominator: 504 eligible coded tweets (a random sample of 1,200 was drawn from 6,366 tweets captured by the keyword string; 504 met the eligibility criterion of pertaining to the relationship between food and genes)
estimates.definition: Codebook item 'Misleading or incorrect information', value 'Incorrect information'; assessed by two genetics/nutrition experts, fact-checked when unclear.
estimates.misinfo_def: "Misleading or incorrect information | Potentially misleading, Incorrect information, Neither | Determined by secondary coding process and fact-checking where needed" (Table 1 codebook)
estimates.source_quote: Overall, 29% (146/504) of tweets were judged to contain potentially misleading information, 14.9% (75/504) contained untrue information, and the remaining 56.2% (283/504) had neither ( Table 4 ).
estimates.page_loc: Results, 'Results by Presence of Potentially Misleading or Untrue Content'; Table 4
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Following initial coding by 4 trained coders (Krippendorff alpha >= .67 on 10% of the data set for all other variables), authors SB and SP - experts on genetics and nutrition - assessed ALL tweets for potentially misleading information and separately for false information, fact-checking unclear cases; all disagreements resolved by discussion against the scientific literature; all tweets double-coded for these variables with kappa at or above the 0.6 benchmark.
estimates.moderator_quote: We used Twitter Archiver [ 49 ] to capture all tweets over a 3-month period from September 1, 2020, to December 1, 2020, which contained combinations of keywords represented by the search string ([genes OR genetics OR DNA OR nutrigenomics OR nutrigenetics] AND [diet OR nutrition OR eating OR food OR slimming]) to capture tweets related to the intersection of genetics and diet. This process resulted in 6366 tweets. A random sample of 1200 tweets was created by sorting the data according to a random number.
estimates.notes: denom_scope=topical (single-issue keyword corpus: the intersection of genetics and diet), denom_selection='' because the 1,200 were a RANDOM sample of the keyword corpus, not a top-N/most-viewed/curated multi-issue selection. Country is not reported; tweets only had to be in English, so country_norm=Global. Eligibility attrition is large (1,200 sampled -> 504 coded), i.e. the denominator is topic-eligible tweets, not all captured tweets.

estimates.notes: JUDGEMENT CALL. The three categories are MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE and sum to 504 (146 + 75 + 283), so 29% is NOT a superset of the 14.9% row - it is the looser-veracity category on its own. I did not create a combined 'misleading or untrue' row because 43.9% would be a cross-category sum I computed, which R8 forbids. Kept as CONTENT (the codebook item is explicit false/misleading coding with expert fact-checking), but flagged borderline because 'POTENTIALLY misleading' can attach to hype-type statements that are not themselves false; an adjudicator preferring the strict tie-break could reclassify this row as QUALITY. definition_variant=true (same country x platform cell, looser veracity threshold).

missed_or_uncertain: NOT EXTRACTED: (1) The cross-tabulations in Table 4 give the topic and expertise composition WITHIN the misleading/untrue/neither columns (e.g. of the 75 untrue tweets, 32 (43%) were about nutrigenomics concepts). Those are column percentages of the misinformation set, not prevalence within a topic denominator, so no within_misinfo_content row is derivable without recomputation - the paper does not report 'x% of nutrigenomics tweets were untrue'. (2) The combined 'misleading OR untrue' share (43.9%) is not reported by the paper and would be a computed cross-category sum, so it is excluded per R8. (3) 26.2% (132/504) of tweet authors presented as science/medicine experts, 74 (15%) tweets contained a product link, 199 (39%) an information-source link - author/content descriptors, not misinformation shares. (4) Engagement means (retweets 1.04, likes 4.13, followers 11,449.58) are per-tweet averages, not shares. (5) No country breakdown is available - the corpus was restricted only to English-language tweets.

rob.design: Twitter Archiver capture of all tweets 1 Sep - 1 Dec 2020 matching a genetics x diet keyword string (6,366 tweets); random sample of 1,200; 504 eligible after coder-applied eligibility screening (English, human genetics AND food/eating/body weight). 4 trained coders coded all tweets for the general codebook (Krippendorff alpha >= .67 on 10% double-coded); the misleading/untrue variables were coded separately by two subject-matter-expert authors on ALL tweets, double-coded, kappa >= 0.6, disagreements resolved by discussion with fact-checking. Limitations: single platform, keyword-defined corpus, no country or user-level sampling frame, engagement metrics missing for deleted tweets.
